t: LeetCode 1812 - Determine Color of a Chessboard Square: One Parity Check
o: Chessboard colors alternate: stepping one column or one row always flips the color, exactly like a checkerboard. Number the columns a-h as 0-7 and the rows 1-8 as 0-7; then the square (file, rank) is white exactly when file + rank is odd. Checking the examples: a1 is (0,0), even, hence black; h3 is (7,2), odd, hence white; c7 is (2,6), even, hence black. Since the input is guaranteed to be a valid two-character coordinate, letter first, no validation is needed and the whole task collapses to a single parity test.
k: Square color: white iff column index + row index is odd (equivalently their parities differ).
Adding raw character codes works too, because a and 1 are both odd letters/digits whose constant contribution cancels mod 2.
Parity of a sum equals the XOR of the parities, enabling a branch-free bit trick.

a.i: Convert the letter and digit to numbers and test whether their sum is odd. Even cheaper, add the raw character codes directly: since a and 1 are both odd, their fixed contribution is even, so code-sum parity equals offset-sum parity.
s: Add their character codes (or converted offsets)
Return true (white) iff the sum is odd

a.i: Only the last bit of each character code matters, and parity-of-sum equals XOR of low bits. So compute (letter ^ digit) & 1 with no addition or modulo at all - a neat micro-optimization to mention after the straightforward version.
s: That bit is 1 exactly for white squares

w: Lead with the sum-parity formula and offer the XOR variant as a flourish; anything heavier (hash sets of white squares, simulating the board) is overkill. Pitfall: mixing up 0-indexed versus 1-indexed rows - harmless here precisely because the fixed bases cancel, but worth explaining. Follow-ups: generalize to larger boards, or answer whether two given squares share a color (same formula applied twice).
